events.content: Equinix Q2 2026 total revenue and segment results recent filing

Equinix has not yet filed or reported **Q3 2026** as of October 17, 2026: its investor-relations filing page identifies the latest quarterly filing as the **Q2 2026 Form 10-Q**, filed July 29, 2026, while Q3 earnings are scheduled for October 28, 2026. [[1, 2]] 

In the latest reported quarter, **Q2 2026 (three months ended June 30, 2026)**, Equinix generated **$2.625 billion of total revenue**, up **16% year over year** from **$2.256 billion**. [[3, 4]]

| Q2 2026 segment result | Revenue ($m) | Recurring revenue ($m) | Non-recurring revenue ($m) | Segment adjusted EBITDA ($m) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Americas | 1,251 | 1,067 | 184 | 641 |
| EMEA | 845 | 806 | 39 | 456 |
| Asia-Pacific | 529 | 504 | 25 | 299 |
| **Total** | **2,625** | **2,377** | **248** | **1,396** |

The figures above are from Equinix’s Q2 2026 Form 10-Q, which defines the company’s three reportable geographic segments as Americas, EMEA, and Asia-Pacific and reports revenue and adjusted EBITDA by segment. [[4]] 

Americas was the largest and fastest-growing segment, with revenue up **$247 million, or 25% year over year**, to $1.251 billion; EMEA revenue rose **$78 million, or 10%**, to $845 million; and Asia-Pacific revenue rose **$44 million, or 9%**, to $529 million. [[4]] 

For context only, Equinix’s Q2 release guided to **Q3 2026 revenue of $2.525 billion to $2.575 billion**, rather than reporting a Q3 actual result. [[3]]

tool_arguments.query: Equinix Q2 2026 AI-related data-center leasing xScale demand revenue figure

events.content: Equinix Q2 2026 AI-related data-center leasing xScale demand revenue figure

**Q2 2026 read-through:** Equinix’s xScale leasing demand was exceptionally strong: it signed **134 MW of xScale leases across the Americas** during Q2, demonstrating substantial hyperscale capacity absorption. [[1]] 

The xScale platform had **604 MW leased** across its current portfolio at quarter-end, versus more than **2,000 MW of total capacity when fully built out**, indicating a large remaining development runway but also meaningful execution, power-availability, and preleasing requirements. [[1]] 

The Hampton transaction was included in the 134 MW and generated approximately **$120 million of non-recurring fees**, which was a material contributor to Q2’s reported **16% year-over-year revenue growth** to **$2.625 billion**. [[2]] [[3]] 

Demand was not limited to xScale: Equinix reported **23% year-over-year annualized gross-bookings growth**, its second-highest volume on record, and a record sold-but-not-yet-installed backlog. [[3]] 

Management also reported that about **30% of remaining 2026 retail expansion capacity had been pre-sold** and that more than **45% of its Q3 bookings target** had already closed, supporting a broader view of tight, accelerating demand across both retail colocation and hyperscale-oriented capacity. [[2]] 

AI is an important demand driver, but Equinix did **not** disclose what portion of the 134 MW xScale signings was specifically AI-related; its formal commentary instead characterized customer demand as broad-based across networking, cloud, and AI infrastructure. [[3]] 

The practical implication is favorable for xScale growth and monetization: Equinix is accelerating more than **7,000 cabinets** that had been scheduled for 2027 into **Q4 2026**, while lifting its full-year revenue-growth guidance to **11%–12%** from **10%–11%**. [[1]] 

Investors should normalize the quarter for the Hampton-related fee, however, because the company explicitly attributed part of Q2 revenue and profit growth to one-time xScale fees rather than recurring leasing revenue. [[3]] [[2]]

events.content: Equinix short seller report Hindenburg Muddy Waters Citron latest allegations 2024 2025

**Hindenburg’s short report on Equinix (NASDAQ: EQIX)** was published on **March 20, 2024**, under the title *“Equinix Exposed: Major Accounting Manipulation, Core Business Decay And Selling An AI Pipe Dream As Insiders Cashed Out Hundreds of Millions.”* [[1]]

**The core allegation was that Equinix materially overstated adjusted funds from operations (AFFO), a key non-GAAP/REIT cash-flow metric, by at least 22% in 2023.** [[1]] Hindenburg alleged that the principal mechanism was misclassifying recurring maintenance capital expenditure as non-recurring/growth capital expenditure, which reduces the AFFO deduction for maintenance spending and raises reported AFFO. [[1]] 

Hindenburg further alleged that Equinix capitalized operating expenses that should have been expensed, inflating both reported operating profitability and AFFO. [[1]] It argued that the alleged accounting choices were economically significant because executive compensation incorporated AFFO targets, and claimed executives had received compensation linked to those metrics while insiders sold substantial amounts of stock. [[1]] [[2]] 

The report also challenged the strategic narrative around AI, contending that power constraints and competition/commoditization in Equinix’s traditional colocation and interconnection business limited its ability to benefit from AI-related data-center demand. [[3]] [[1]] Hindenburg said its work included reviews of financial and litigation records plus interviews with **37 former employees, industry experts and competitors**. [[1]]

**Market and company response:** EQIX closed down **2.3% to $824.88** on the publication day after trading as low as $796.90, according to contemporaneous reporting. [[3]] Equinix initially said it was reviewing the assertions, then announced on **March 25, 2024** that its Audit Committee had begun an independent investigation. [[3]] [[4]] 

Equinix subsequently disclosed that it received a subpoena from the **U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of California** shortly after the report and, on **April 30, 2024**, a subpoena from the **SEC**. [[5]] [[6]] Its March 2025 Form 10-Q stated that it was cooperating fully with both agencies. [[6]]

events.content: Equinix Q1 2026 earnings call AI data-center leasing demand xScale revenues

**Q2 2026 takeaway:** Equinix characterized demand as broad-based and stronger than its prior long-term planning assumptions, with demand split between large enterprises modernizing legacy on-premises infrastructure and net-new AI-native workloads/service providers. [[1]]

- Equinix closed **134 MW of xScale leases** in Q2 2026, including the Hampton transaction, which generated roughly **$120 million of non-recurring fees**. [[1]]
- Management said **“the vast majority” of its largest Q2 deals were driven by AI workloads**, consistent with the prior several quarters. [[1]]
- Importantly, the company did **not** disclose that all 134 MW of xScale leasing was AI-specific; the more supportable reading is that AI is a major demand accelerant across its portfolio, while xScale leasing activity includes hyperscale capacity transactions such as Hampton. [[1]]
- The strength translated into a capacity-response plan: Equinix added nine projects since April and had **52 projects underway across 33 markets** at quarter-end. [[2]]
- Q2 revenue was **$2.625 billion**, up **16% year over year**, with growth aided by underlying execution and one-time xScale fees. [[3]]
- Management’s practical demand signal was raised outlook and an accelerated expansion program, with long-term annual capex envisioned at **$5 billion–$7 billion**, excluding real-estate acquisitions and xScale. [[1]]

**Bottom line:** The transcript supports a bullish AI-led leasing thesis—AI drove most large deals and is helping sustain capacity demand—but it does not support equating the full 134 MW of Q2 xScale leases directly to AI demand. [[1]]

private_messages.content:
**Q2 2026 takeaway:** Equinix characterized demand as broad-based and stronger than its prior long-term planning assumptions, with demand split between large enterprises modernizing legacy on-premises infrastructure and net-new AI-native workloads/service providers. [[1]]

- Equinix closed **134 MW of xScale leases** in Q2 2026, including the Hampton transaction, which generated roughly **$120 million of non-recurring fees**. [[1]]
- Management said **“the vast majority” of its largest Q2 deals were driven by AI workloads**, consistent with the prior several quarters. [[1]]
- Importantly, the company did **not** disclose that all 134 MW of xScale leasing was AI-specific; the more supportable reading is that AI is a major demand accelerant across its portfolio, while xScale leasing activity includes hyperscale capacity transactions such as Hampton. [[1]]
- The strength translated into a capacity-response plan: Equinix added nine projects since April and had **52 projects underway across 33 markets** at quarter-end. [[2]]
- Q2 revenue was **$2.625 billion**, up **16% year over year**, with growth aided by underlying execution and one-time xScale fees. [[3]]
- Management’s practical demand signal was raised outlook and an accelerated expansion program, with long-term annual capex envisioned at **$5 billion–$7 billion**, excluding real-estate acquisitions and xScale. [[1]]

**Bottom line:** The transcript supports a bullish AI-led leasing thesis—AI drove most large deals and is helping sustain capacity demand—but it does not support equating the full 134 MW of Q2 xScale leases directly to AI demand. [[1]]
